30476.etyen:
From the surname of the German priest and naturopath Sebastian Kneipp + brød (“bread”), named after Kneipp and a bread recipe associated with him. The bread was introduced in Norway in 1895 by Baker Hansen, which had received Kneipp's approval to bake and sell it according to his recipe.
The second element, brød, is the Danish-form word from Old Danish brøth (“bread”), corresponding to Old Norse brauð (“bread”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk kneippbrød and Swedish kneippbröd (“Kneipp bread”).

111116.etyen:
From Nord-Makedonia (“North Macedonia”) + -er (“demonym-forming suffix”), with loss of the final -ia. The country name is from Nord- (“north”) + Makedonia (“Macedonia”).
The second element is ultimately from Ancient Greek Μᾰκεδονῐ́ᾱ (Măkedonĭ́ā, “Macedonia”), from Μᾰκεδών (Măkedṓn, “a Macedonian”) and the place-name suffix -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā). The ethnonym is traditionally connected with μᾰκεδνός (măkednós, “tall, tapering”); a derivation of that adjective from Pre-Greek has also been proposed.
Parallel formations include Norwegian Nynorsk nordmakedonar and nordmakedoniar, Danish nordmakedoner and nor

1000460.etyen:
Internationalism, ultimately from Medieval Latin Serbia (“Serbia”). The name belongs to the same word family as Serbo-Croatian Ср̏бин (“Serb”) and ultimately continues Proto-Slavic *sьrbъ (“Serb; Sorb”). The Proto-Slavic ethnonym has been connected with Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to protect, watch over”), though its deeper origin remains uncertain.
Compare Serbo-Croatian Ср̀бија (“Serbia”). Parallel international forms include Norwegian Nynorsk Serbia, Danish Serbien, Swedish Serbien, German Serbien, Dutch Servië, French Serbie, Italian Serbia, Spanish Serbia, Portuguese Sérvia, Polish Serbia

1004044.etyen:
Corresponding to -bo, from bo (“to live, dwell”), from Old Norse búa (“to live, dwell”). In botanical terminology, the element is used with prefixes such as en- (“one”), sam- (“together, same”), sær- (“separate”) and tve- (“two”) to describe whether male and female reproductive organs occur on the same plant or on separate plants.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -bu and Danish -bo (“botany suffix”).
